name: PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: London Sumatra — an estate the market barely pays for
frontmatter.summary: A mature planter whose cash is most of its market value, and whose estate the market barely pays for. We stay BUY at Rp3,750 (155.6%), restating the trapped-cash discount on the September related-party balance and charging it at even odds. The November DHE SDA relaxation changes no input: LSIP's palm sales are domestic and direct exports a sliver [S17, S7].
thesis: Cash of IDR8,516.3bn and no interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 is most of the IDR10,264.0bn market capitalisation [S8, F37].
A mature estate earned 43.5% EBITDA margins at the deck price, with most output sold domestically to the parent at a persistent discount to the export benchmark [S7, S15].
The dividend is covered at a thirty per cent payout and a IDR750.0bn buyback is running; neither is capitalised in the target [S12, S9].
The DCF, the config-blend multiples and book value all sit far above the price; the reverse DCF implies CPO near US$831/t [S0].
The risk is structural: related-party offtake, a controlling holder with no obligation to distribute, and a payout already cut once [S7, S12, S13].

catalysts.event: Implementing finance-ministry regulation for the DHE SDA conversion amendment; no direct effect on LSIP, watched only for the exchange-rate channel
Buyback window closes; B50 biodiesel mandate and the monthly CPO export levy reset
FY2026 audited results and the final dividend declaration for the year
First-half production and the El Nino impact on FFB yields

blocks.text: **Update, 9 November 2026.** This revision restates the trapped-cash discount on the 30 September 2026 related-party balance, recomputes the retained-cash item on the current enterprise value without double-counting the July dividend, returns the cross-checks to the config blend, and sources the cost of equity to the macro inputs. The DHE SDA relaxation changes no input: palm and seed sales are domestic rupiah sales and direct exports were IDR43.7bn of a IDR5,511.7bn base [S7, S17]. The target fell because peer medians and the exchange rate refreshed, not because the price did; the price is Rp1,505 on 6 November 2026 [S0].

London Sumatra is a mid-sized Indonesian oil-palm estate owned by the Indofood group, priced as though the estate were a liability attached to a pile of cash. At Rp1,505 the company is worth about IDR10,264.0bn, against IDR8,516.3bn of cash and no interest-bearing debt at 30 September 2026 [S8]; the market pays barely more than the cash pile for the estate and mills.

That is not a distressed business. At the deck price the estate earned an EBITDA margin of 43.5%, a net profit of IDR1,887.8bn and Rp277 per share in the last audited year [S7], and the first nine months were better: net profit rose by two fifths [S3, S8].

Our target is Rp3,750, 155.6% above the price: a DCF at the through-cycle deck price plus cash net of a probability-weighted governance discount, corroborated by two multiples at the config blend. The reverse DCF is the discipline: the price implies CPO of US$831/t at the reference year against a deck of 1,240.0 USD/t [S0, S15] — either the deck is wrong or the cash never reaches shareholders.

PT Perusahaan Perkebunan London Sumatra Indonesia Tbk is one of Indonesia's oldest plantation companies, with nucleus estates in North Sumatra, South Sumatra, East Kalimantan, Java and Sulawesi [S6]. It sold 290.0 kt CPO of CPO from a nucleus planted area of just over one hundred and ten thousand hectares — about ninety-one thousand oil palm, sixteen thousand rubber and the balance cocoa and tea, with roughly seven per cent of the oil palm immature — and manages about thirty-five thousand hectares of plasma estates [S6].

The company reports three segments. Oil palm products, crude palm oil and palm kernel, are the overwhelming majority of revenue; SumBio seeds and a small rubber, cocoa and tea residual make up the rest [S7]. There is no refining of consequence: this is an upstream grower and miller, so its economics are the spread between the CPO price and the cost of a tonne.

More than three fifths of revenue is sold to PT Salim Ivomas Pratama, the listed subsidiary of Indofood Agri Resources that controls London Sumatra; including other related parties, almost two thirds moves within the group, and only a sliver is exported [S7]. Sales are market-referenced, and the audited realisation was stable against the export benchmark across the two audited years, which suggests a structural domestic discount, not arbitrary transfer pricing; the lower 2026 tape is the basis for our forecast [S7, S15]. Strategy is replanting, yield recovery and cost control: capex is a steady share of revenue, planted area has drifted down over five years, and there is no announced expansion or downstream project [S6].

Group structure matters here. The Salim family controls the company through Salim Ivomas and Indofood Agri Resources, with a free float of 40.0% [S13, S0]. All 6,820 m shares are listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange; no special-monitoring-board designation or notation letter appears in the filings and disclosures we hold, and the shares are not suspended [S7, S8]. That ownership explains both the stable offtake and the persistent discount this report is about.

Indonesia is the world's largest CPO producer, and the price London Sumatra receives is set globally. The deck has CPO averaging 1,135.0 USD/t this year, rising next year and easing toward a long-run anchor of 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with Indonesian inflation [S0, S15]. The near-term premium reflects tight balances and the expectation that El Nino will depress yields into next year; beyond that the deck assumes supply responds and the market settles toward marginal cost [S11].

Policy is active. Indonesia taxes CPO exports through a levy plus duty that moves monthly with a reference price; for November the combined charge fell by a fifth to 246.4 USD/t per tonne [S10]. The levy is borne by the exporter and matters here only at the margin because sales are domestic. The biodiesel mandate matters more: the move from a forty to a fifty per cent blend is the largest source of incremental domestic demand and underpins the government's willingness to keep export charges high [S10].

The live exchange-control change is separate and is not a palm-price policy. Under PP 21/2026, in force since June, non-oil-and-gas exporters must bring all DHE SDA onshore for at least twelve months, with conversion into rupiah capped at half; a fourth amendment to PP 36/2023 would lift that toward all of it, with implementing rules due by end-November [S17, S16]. It changes the currency in which the onshore balance may be held, not the dollars received or the duty to repatriate them, and its incidence here is negligible: palm and seed revenue is rupiah revenue from a domestic customer, and direct exports were IDR43.7bn of a IDR5,511.7bn base [S7]. The one channel it reaches LSIP through is the exchange rate. CPO is priced in dollars and costed in rupiah; the sensitivity grid in section four shows a two per cent move in the rupiah shifting the twelve-month value about two and a half per cent. That is real but second-order, and the regulation is not an exchange-rate forecast, so no input changes [S17, S0].

Competition is a cost-curve story: listed peers compete on yield, age profile and distance to mill, not brand. London Sumatra's estates are old, with a large mature base and a continuing replanting need; its cash cost of 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne rose because external FFB purchases climbed by more than a third [S7, S6]. It survives a trough on its balance sheet rather than its cost position. The moat is land and logistics — HGU rights, mills, plasma partnerships and the parent's refining system — real barriers to entry that do not protect margins from a falling price [S6]. Five forces are unfavourable on the customer side, neutral on suppliers and favourable against new entrants [S6]. The variables that matter are the CPO price, the rupiah and the weather.

The data pack misstates the last audited year. Revenue rose 20.8% to IDR5,511.7bn on higher CPO volume and price and recovered palm kernel revenue; operating profit was IDR2,008.4bn and net profit to the parent IDR1,887.8bn [S7]. The pack's depreciation is unusable — a few billion rupiah against the audited IDR389.5bn — so we key the audited figure, lift FY2025 EBITDA to IDR2,397.8bn and the margin to 43.5%, restate FY2024 the same way, and strike every multiple off this base [S7, F12].

The cash cost is 7,791,431 rupiah per tonne, backed out of audited cost of sales after removing depreciation and allocating cost to the other lines; it rose because external FFB purchases climbed by more than a third, and we hold it in real terms and escalate with inflation [S7]. Realisation is calibrated on the nine-month interim: CPO revenue over CPO volume gives a dollar price flat against the prior year while the benchmark rose, a ratio of 75.8% [S8, S3, S0]. The gap to the audited 858.1 USD/t against 1,007.0 USD/t is the domestic reference lag, not a series break: LSIP invoices against the Harga Referensi, which averaged 14,234 rupiah per kilogram [S10, F41].

Revenue rises to IDR5,988.9bn this year, with EBITDA IDR2,684.3bn, net profit IDR2,189.5bn and Rp321 per share; the margin peaks with the deck and compresses as price eases and costs escalate. Volume is held at 300 kt because the estate is mature [S0, S7]. Calibration reads negative for the same domestic-reference reason: at the current-year benchmark the model's dollar ASP of 860.3 USD/t is flat against last year's realised 858.1 USD/t, which is the like-for-like test [S8, S3, S15].

Capex runs at 7.9% of revenue, working capital is small and most EBITDA becomes cash [S7]: IDR8,516.3bn at the third quarter against zero interest-bearing debt and no refinancing risk [S8]. The dividend is Rp83 at a thirty per cent payout and the buyback is a further return of capital [S12, S9]. Operating cash flow of IDR3,015.7bn exceeded net profit, so the accruals ratio is negative through the three years [S7, S0]. The flag is inventories, up to IDR830.8bn, a build of about a third against a tenth of revenue growth that one quarter explains but a second would not [S8, S3]. Biological-asset fair-value swings are non-cash, tax is below headline on recurring permanent differences, and the opinion is unmodified [S7].

We use a DCF as the primary method, with EV/EBITDA and P/BV cross-checks at the industry weights of sixty, twenty-five and fifteen per cent — the method set for a price-taking grower whose value is the cash a mature asset earns over a cycle. Terminal growth is 2.5%, long-run rupiah inflation [S0].

The cost of equity is 11.2%: the rupiah ten-year yield of 7.4% [S18], a beta of 0.80 times the mature premium of 4.2% plus the country premium of 2.5%, net of the 1.6% sovereign default spread [S19]; with no net debt WACC equals it. The beta is the industry config default, not a measured regression — the house beta file holds a coal median only. It does not decide the rating: a beta a tenth above the default cuts the target about a twenty-fifth and one a quarter above about a fourteenth.

The DCF gives Rp4,012 per share, a terminal value of 46.0% of it, on an enterprise value of IDR24,513.3bn plus September net cash and the associate. The terminal capitalises the deck anchor of 1,150.0 USD/t in FY2029 money escalated with inflation, so the first terminal year is 1,178.8 USD/t, not the 1,180.0 USD/t print [S0, S15]. The anchor sits a fifth above the FY2023 to FY2025 average of 952.0 USD/t and a seventh above the last actual; that premium is disclosed and not added again.

The cross-checks use the config blend of peer median and own history, as the red team insisted. EV/EBITDA blends to 5.7x and gives Rp2,432; P/BV blends the peer median with an own average that is itself below book, to 1.1x, and gives Rp2,367. The earlier peer-median-only P/BV leg is withdrawn because it lifted a cross-check to the level the thesis was forecasting. Both sit below the DCF — the EBITDA leg by about a third, the book leg by about two fifths. They are struck off one year's EBITDA and historical-cost book, and the EBITDA leg is charged the full governance bridge against a metric that already holds the cash. If the estate never re-rates, the multiples are the better guide, and even they are far above the price.

The bridge adds the balance sheet at face and subtracts a probability-weighted trapped-cash discount on the opening balance of IDR8,516.3bn and on the cash the DCF retains, so the growing cash inside the operating value is charged at the same rate. The opening item uses the September balance, the engine's net-debt date; the retained item is derived from the current-run enterprise value of IDR24,513.3bn and the dividend stream from September onward with the terminal dividend, and excludes the FY2025 dividend paid in July, which is already inside September cash.

In the persistent state the balance and the deposit at the related bank are never withdrawn, so cash is worth about two fifths of face. The September accounts restate the evidence: related-party cash IDR665.0bn, 4.0% of assets and under a tenth of the cash balance, against a tenth of assets at the year-end [S8, F53, F54], with IDR7,629.3bn of third-party time deposits at Danamon, OCBC NISP and Mega [S8, F57]. We charge the whole balance, not only the related-party slice, because the holder sets cash policy for every account. Even odds stand on evidence both ways: the payout was cut from thirty-five to thirty per cent and there is no minority veto, but every year has been paid and a buyback is running [S12, S9, S13].

Because both items scale with that probability, the ladder is about a quarter higher at zero, an eighth higher at one in four, an eighth lower at three in four and about a quarter lower at certainty. The bear with the trap at certainty is about three fifths of the current price — the state in which this investment loses money. That state is quoted, not run: the bridge probability is one input shared by all scenarios [S12, S13].

A step-up to the sister's fifty per cent payout would raise the present value of dividends by two thirds, cut the retained haircut by two fifths and add about a fifteenth. A buyback of IDR750.0bn, running from 26 October to 31 December 2026 on internal cash [S9], retires about seven per cent of the shares at the current price and adds about a twentieth. Together about an eighth of the target; neither is in it.

The reverse DCF is the most useful output. The price implies CPO of about US$831/t at the reference year — two thirds of the deck's 1,240.0 USD/t and an eighth below the FY2023 to FY2025 average [S0, S15] — or, after crediting cash at seven tenths of face, about one and a quarter times last year's EBITDA; at face cash, about three quarters of a time. Either the market expects CPO far below the deck, or it expects the cash to be consumed by the group; we think both, partly mitigated by the dividend and buyback. The price grid is struck through a CPO override that holds later years flat, so it sits a little under a tenth below the base at its centre; read it for the slope and take the level from the base case.

The largest risk is the one we are implicitly betting against: that the discount is permanent. London Sumatra is a controlled subsidiary of a family group, most output is sold to its parent, and a material share of cash sits with a related bank — IDR665.0bn, 4.0% of total assets, withdrawable at the group's discretion [S8, F53]. Minority shareholders cannot force a distribution, the payout has been cut once, and a value investor can be right about the asset and wrong about the exit for years. That is the value-trap configuration; we charge for it explicitly rather than framing the thesis around a re-rating.

The second risk is CPO. The base uses the house deck, which embeds a near-term El Nino premium; if the weather fades and Malaysian stocks rebuild, price could fall by a quarter or more and the operating value with it [S11]. The bear models that with a volume shortfall, a working-capital stretch and a real cost base a fifth above the last actual. The third cluster is operational and regulatory: external FFB purchases are a flexible cost but a source of margin volatility, and the levy and biodiesel mandate change the domestic price [S10]. A weaker rupiah helps the rupiah price but raises imported fertiliser and fuel costs. None is existential for a debt-free producer, but each moves earnings enough to matter for a stock priced on sentiment.

Two downsides are sized. FY2024 carried a IDR296.2bn impairment of the rubber plantations against a fixed-asset carrying amount of about five trillion rupiah, and the same assets could be written down again under the bear's conditions [S7]. The related-party cash, at IDR665.0bn, is a twenty-fifth of total assets; a run on that relationship would remove a visible slice of liquidity in one step.

Daily turnover is about IDR17.6bn and the free float is 40.0%, above the fund's floor, so the engine applies no liquidity discount; the constraint is ownership and willingness to distribute [S0, S13].

The scenarios mirror the base shock for shock. The bear holds CPO at the FY2023 trough of 886.0 USD/t at the reference year [S15], with volume down about a sixth, the real cost base up a fifth and working capital stretched; it charges the trapped-cash discount at even odds, so it is an operating bear rather than a governance state. It still produces a value above the current price — Rp1,793, about a third above — and that is the point: even at the cycle's realised low the market pays less than the estate alone is worth. What loses money here is not a lower CPO path but a transfer of value out of the minority's hands: with the trap at certainty the same bear is about three fifths of the current price, as quantified in section four. One distortion is disclosed: the retained-cash item is a single absolute amount computed on the base and applied to all three runs, so the published bear is charged several times its own retained cash and the bull less than half; on each scenario's own value the bear would be about a quarter higher and the bull about a tenth lower, and the base is within two per cent. The bull raises price by two fifths, volume about a sixth, releases working capital and holds costs a sixth below the last actual; it is deliberately not the capital-return state, because a payout the base does not assume would flatter it. The probability-weighted target is Rp3,750. The signposts that would change our view are a sustained CPO break below the bear, a related-party transaction that transfers cash out below market value, another payout cut, or the buyback being abandoned.

The controlling shareholder is PT Salim Ivomas Pratama, part of the Indofood Agri Resources group, holding just under three fifths of the shares; Indofood Agri holds a small direct stake [S13]. The free float is 40.0% of the 6,820 m shares, and the pack records insider ownership near 70.0%, overlapping with the group's indirect holdings [S0, S13]. We find no share-pledge disclosure in the audited accounts or the interim, no control contest and no restatement, and the board comprises group nominees alongside independent commissioners [S7, S8].

Related-party dealings are the central governance fact. Sales of more than three fifths of revenue to the parent, FFB purchases from related estates, finance income on deposits at a related bank and group service companies all appear in the notes [S7]. Each is disclosed at market-referenced terms, and the audited realisation discount to the export benchmark was stable across the two audited years, the best available evidence that terms are not manipulated; the lower 2026 tape is treated as the domestic-reference effect [S7, S15]. It is still a structure in which the minority depends on the holder's goodwill, and the market prices that dependence.

The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, with an unmodified opinion and no qualification or change of auditor of note [S7]. The company does not revalue its plantations, so book value is conservative and understates replacement cost, which is why P/BV is a floor rather than a target. The dividend record is the main counterweight: a payout every year, thirty per cent of profit for the last two years and thirty-five before [S12]. The cut is why the trap probability stays at even odds rather than lower.

On ESG the exposures are land and deforestation, peat, labour and smallholder relations. The estates are long established, the company operates plasma partnerships, the industry's main social-licence mechanism, and reports against the national sustainability standard [S6]. Transition risk is low relative to social and regulatory risk.

The near-term catalyst is the full-year result and the dividend declaration that follows. The interim showed profit up two fifths and cash higher, so the base for the final dividend is strong [S3, S8]; a dividend at the policy ratio would raise the yield on the current price.

The buyback runs from 26 October to 31 December 2026 on internal cash [S9]; execution at the current price is accretive because the shares trade below the cash they represent. We treat completion as upside, because the size is a ceiling and nothing commits the company to the full amount.

Third is policy: the B50 mandate and the monthly export levy reset determine the domestic CPO price and the group's offtake economics [S10]. The implementing regulation for the DHE SDA conversion change is due by end-November, watched only for the exchange-rate channel [S17].

The operational signposts are FFB output, extraction rate and external FFB purchases; the first nine months showed recovery on all three [S3], and a reversal would test the bear. The El Nino lag is the main reason to expect a weaker patch, which we would treat as an opportunity provided the cash return continues. Above all we monitor related-party flows: any change in the offtake, the deposit relationship or the group's willingness to let cash accumulate matters more to the equity than the CPO price [S7, S13].

valuation.label: P/BV
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The discount persists and the cycle troughs at the same time. The controlling shareholder keeps the cash inside the group - the trapped-cash discount is charged at even odds in every scenario, and the fixed rupiah amount is therefore a larger share of a lower bear value - and related-party cash at Bank Ina Perdana of Rp665.016bn at 30-Sep-2026 is not withdrawn [S8, F53]. On top of that, CPO is held at 71.5% of the deck for the whole forecast, which is USD 886/t at the FY2027E reference year - the FY2023 trough of the World Bank Pink Sheet series [S15] - and about USD 812/t in the current year, well below the FY2023-25 realised average of USD 952/t and the deck anchor [S0]. The El Nino premium unwinds and Malaysian stocks rebuild [S11], a weaker FFB crop cuts volume 15% from the 300 kt plan, external FFB and fertiliser prices push the real cash cost 20% above the FY2025 level, and the parent receivable stretches working capital 30% [F34]. With the trap at certainty instead of even odds this operating bear is worth Rp869, below the current price: that is the governance-failure state, and it is quoted in section 5 rather than run as a fourth scenario because the bridge probability is a single model input shared by all scenarios.

bull.narrative: A severe El Nino and the B50 mandate lift CPO two fifths above the deck, as they did in the 2021-22 squeeze [S10, S11]; a normal Q4, the maturing 6,054 ha of immature oil palm and a yield recovery from the weather-depressed base take volume 17.6% above the 300 kt plan; faster collection from SIMP releases working capital; and the extraction-rate and FFB-purchase programme hold the real cash cost a sixth below the FY2025 level [S3]. The capital-return levers the report calls the route to value are quantified outside the scenario shocks and are not in the value above: a step-up to the group sister's 50% payout adds about Rp258 per share and the Rp750bn buyback, running 26-Oct to 31-Dec-2026 on internal cash [S9], about Rp206 per share as it retires 7.3% of the shares at Rp1,505. They are not shocked here because the payout is a board decision the base case does not assume and the buyback size is a ceiling, not an executed amount.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the 9M-2026 run-rate plus a normal Q4: CPO sales were 222 kt in the nine months (+7% yoy, [S3]) and Q4-2025 was 82.5 kt of the 290 kt year [F1], giving about 300 kt. Production supports it: 9M-2026 CPO output rose 12% to 227 kt on nucleus FFB up 7% to 850 kt [S3], and FY2025 production was 292 kt [F33]. The estate is mature and not expanding: nucleus oil palm is 90,798 ha with only 7% immature [F32], so the plan is held flat at 300 kt with no yield-growth assumption, inside the 15% drift gate. FY2025 sales of 290 kt are the last audited actual [F1].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Recalibrated on the last actual, the 9M-2026 interim. CPO (MKS) revenue of Rp3,342.357bn [S8, F48] over 222 kt of CPO sales [S3, F47] is Rp15.056m per tonne; at the model's FY2026E usd_idr of 17,570 [S0] that is USD 856.9/t against the deck's 9M-2026 average of USD 1,131/t (Q1 1,081, Q2 1,164, Q3 1,148, [S15]), a realisation of 0.758. The older audited years gave 0.852 (FY2025 Rp14.114m/t against 1,007 at 16,448.09 [F3]; FY2024 the same [F4]); the gap to the 9M-2026 tape is the domestic reference lag, not a series break: LSIP invoices against the government's Harga Referensi at Rp14,234/kg in FY2025 [F41], and the realised dollar price has been flat while the export benchmark rose in 2026, so the last actual is the right denominator and the audited ratio is not. 0.758 is held flat rather than faded, per the last-actual rule. At the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet rate of Rp17,998 [S8] the same revenue/volume is USD 836.5/t, a 0.740 ratio, which brackets the 0.758 estimate from below.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Zero: no DMO-style domestic price cap applies to Indonesian CPO sales in this period; the B40/B50 mandate is a demand driver, not a cap on LSIP's selling price [S10].

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Palm oil cost intensity is expressed per tonne of CPO, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no overburden analogue in a plantation [S7].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne of CPO (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the last audited year and escalated with IDR inflation only. FY2025 COGS of Rp3,250.368bn [F7] less the Rp373.058bn of depreciation inside it [F30] leaves Rp2,877.310bn of cash cost for all products; the non-CPO cost of Rp617.854bn on Rp1,418.588bn of PK, rubber and other revenue at the 56.45% other margin [F28] is stripped out, leaving Rp2,259.456bn of CPO cash cost, or Rp7.791m per tonne on 290 kt [F1]. That is 21% above FY2024's Rp6.420m [F31] because external FFB purchases jumped to Rp672.332bn from Rp488.924bn [S7]; we hold the FY2025 level rather than extrapolate either year. The 2.5% annual escalation is the macro deck's long-run IDR inflation [S0], so the real cost base is flat and the FY2025 gross-margin gain is not assumed to repeat.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar set to zero: the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS, so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S7].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: haulage, milling and port costs are already inside the per-tonne CPO cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [F30]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: 63.26% of revenue is sold domestically to SIMP [F34] and Indonesia's CPO export levy is borne by the exporter at shipment (USD 246.36/t, [F38]), not by LSIP on a domestic sale. The FY2025 cost-of-sales note carries no royalty or export-levy line [S7].

assumptions.label: Other revenue (PK, rubber, others)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 non-CPO revenue was Rp1,418.588bn: palm kernel and related products 1,093.304, rubber 149.982 and others 175.302 [F28]. It is escalated at 2.5% IDR inflation with flat volume, since PK output tracks CPO throughput and rubber prices move with the same cost base [S7, S0]; the FY2024 comparative of Rp921.664bn [F29] was lower because PK prices were weak, not because the product mix changed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: 56.45%: the FY2025 residual implies Rp617.854bn of cost on Rp1,418.588bn of non-CPO revenue once the CPO cash cost is set at Rp7.791m per tonne [F28]. PK and rubber are by-products of FFB already harvested for CPO, so the incremental cost is pressing, handling and freight only; the ratio is held flat.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A of Rp389.453bn (fixed assets 383.284, right-of-use 5.129, deferred charges 1.040, [F13]) over the 300 kt plan is Rp1.298m per tonne. The pack's Rp4.8bn D&A line is defective and has been replaced by the audited Note 25 charge [F13]. The 9M-2026 charge of Rp304.770bn (segment 292.398 plus unallocated 12.372, [S8]) annualises to about Rp406bn, so the FY2025 base is not stale. Escalated at 2.5% IDR; there is no revaluation uplift because LSIP does not apply the PSAK 16 revaluation model [S6].

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 additions to fixed assets were Rp433.312bn [F15], or 7.9% of revenue, spread across replanting, machinery, plasma and infrastructure (segment capex 393.856 plus unallocated 39.456, [S7]); over the 300 kt plan that is Rp1.444m per tonne. The 9M-2026 run-rate of Rp264.471bn [S8] supports the same intensity. Held in real terms with 2.5% IDR escalation rather than assuming a step-down after the current replanting push [S0].

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: LSIP's capex is volume-linked replanting, machinery and plasma support rather than discrete expansion projects, and the planted area has been flat-to-down (110,982 ha in 2025 vs 114,111 ha in 2021, [F32]); all of it is carried in capex_unit.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set at 8%, above the FY2025 actual and well below the FY2024 spike: operating working capital was Rp181.720bn or 3.3% of revenue in FY2025, Rp989.177bn or 21.7% in FY2024 and Rp305.750bn or 7.3% in FY2023 [S0]. It is not the mid-point of that range (12.5%); it is a deliberate conservatism above the last actual. The swing is the receivable from parent SIMP, which is 63.26% of revenue [F34]; 8% keeps the parent receivable funded without assuming the FY2024 build repeats.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 17.2%, the FY2025 effective rate: income tax of Rp391.187bn [F24] on pre-tax profit of Rp2,277.542bn [F9]. Held flat; the 22% headline is reduced by the permanent differences on plasma and land income that recur in the LK [S7].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 8% on a negligible balance: FY2025 finance costs were Rp1.176bn [F23] against lease liabilities of under Rp1bn, and the group carries no bank borrowings at 30-Sep-2026 [F37]. The rate is set so a future lease or drawdown prices sensibly rather than at the engine's 15% clamp.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the three-year average of finance income over opening cash: 5.06% in FY2025 (Rp276.021bn [F21] on Rp5,453.691bn), 4.81% in FY2024 and 4.04% in FY2023 [S0]. The balance is held largely on deposit and partly at related-party Bank Ina Perdana, which supplied Rp44.005bn of FY2025 finance income [S7].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group has no interest-bearing bank debt at 30-Sep-2026, only lease liabilities [F37, S8], and capex plus the dividend are covered by operating cash flow of Rp3,015.733bn in FY2025 [S7]. The announced Rp750bn buyback [S9] is assumed to be funded from cash, not debt.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: no recurring non-operating income or charge is disclosed beyond the associate line (a Rp5.691bn loss in FY2025) and that is immaterial against EBITDA [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: non-controlling interests are Rp3.833bn of a Rp13,999.946bn equity base and their share of profit was a Rp1.401bn loss in FY2025 [S7], so the minority line is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 30%: the company declares 30% of profit, DPS Rp83 for FY2025 and Rp65 for FY2024 on 6,819,963,965 shares [F18, S12]. The FY2025 cash payment of Rp443.234bn was the FY2024 dividend [F17]; the 30% policy is held rather than the engine's default.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: shares outstanding are 6,819,963,965 and unchanged across the audited years [F20]. The Rp750bn buyback announced in October 2026 [S9] is not yet executed and its size is a ceiling, so it is treated as upside in section 5 rather than modelled as a completed reduction.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% nominal IDR, the macro deck's long-run inflation [S0]. With volume flat and CPO prices and costs both escalating at about inflation, real FCFF is flat; a 4% terminal rate would add real growth the business has not shown (nucleus FFB has been flat at 1.34-1.38m tonnes since 2021, [S6]).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue (cash)
assumptions.basis: 4.6%, the FY2025 net operating cost ratio implied by the filing: gross profit Rp2,261.338bn less operating profit Rp2,008.388bn = Rp252.950bn of net operating cost on Rp5,511.706bn of revenue [F11]. It nets other operating income (Rp136.905bn of FX, land-usage and PK-shell income) against selling (Rp73.099bn) and G&A (Rp247.878bn) and the Rp59.571bn bio-asset fair-value loss [S7]. FY2024's 9.7% is not the run-rate because it carries the Rp296.164bn one-off impairment [F12]. Held flat, so no drift.

challenges.challenge: The trapped-cash state is sourced to the 31-Dec-2025 Bank Ina Perdana balance of Rp1,639.556bn (10.55% of total assets), not the 30-Sep-2026 balance. S8 Note 5 shows related-party cash of Rp115.016bn (bank) plus Rp550.000bn (time deposits) = Rp665.016bn, 7.8% of the Rp8,516.274bn cash and 4.0% of the Rp16,766.492bn total assets; the rest sits at third-party banks (Danamon Rp3,078.5bn, OCBC NISP Rp1,500bn, Mega Rp685bn plus USD Rp1,691.8bn). Section 5's "roughly a fifth of the cash balance" and "more than a tenth of total assets" are true only at year-end, and the bridge applies the 58.9% haircut to the September cash as if the year-end concentration still existed.
challenges.answer: Restated to the 30 Sep 2026 balance: related-party cash Rp665.016bn (7.8% of Rp8,516.274bn cash, 3.97% of assets), of which Rp115.016bn bank and Rp550.000bn time deposits, plus Rp7,629.349bn third-party time deposits at Danamon, OCBC NISP and Mega [S8, F53-F57]. The 58.9% haircut is unchanged because it is the deposit yield (4.6%) over the 11.18% cost of equity, not a function of the related-party share. The 0.5 probability is reassessed on the current mix and kept at even odds because the 59.51% holder sets cash policy for every account [S8, S13]. Section 4 now explains why a year-end figure no longer governs.

challenges.challenge: The 0.5 persistence probability is unsourced and untested, yet it drives Rp2,508bn of the opening-cash haircut and Rp4,262bn of the retained-cash haircut. The evidence cuts both ways: a 30% dividend paid every year (S12) and 59.51% control (S13), but the related-party share of cash fell from 21.6% to 7.8% between December and September (S7, S8). Nothing in the record sets 0.5 rather than 0.25 or 0.75.
challenges.answer: The bridge label now gives the full ladder on the current run: target Rp4,711 at probability 0, Rp4,231 at 0.25, Rp3,750 at 0.5 and Rp2,789 at 1.0, with the bear at certainty about Rp832. The 0.5 is set by evidence both ways: every year paid, the FY2025 Rp83 dividend paid 24 Jul 2026 and a buyback running [S12, S9], against the 35% to 30% payout cut and no minority veto [S13]. Section 4 states the ladder and the report cites both directions [S8, S12, S13].

challenges.challenge: The retained-cash bridge item is computed on the prior engine run (EV Rp24,506.23bn, discount factors at asof 2026-11-08), not the current run (EV Rp24,513.35bn at 2026-11-09), and it deducts FY2026E dividends of Rp566.06bn, which are the FY2025 Rp83 dividend paid 24-Jul-2026 (S12) and already inside the 30-Sep-2026 cash (S8: Rp565.976bn paid in 9M-2026). The DCF is stub-aware from 30-Sep (FY2026E fraction 0.252), so the paid dividend is deducted a second time; the retained operating value is understated by about Rp565bn and the haircut over-applied by about Rp166bn (Rp24/share).
challenges.answer: Retained-cash item rebased to the current-run DCF enterprise value of Rp24,513.35bn (asof 9 Nov 2026) and the FY2026E dividend of Rp566.06bn is excluded because it is the FY2025 Rp83 dividend paid 24 Jul 2026, already inside the 30 Sep 2026 cash [S12, S8, F18]. Present value of dividends from FY2027E onward is Rp9,473.30bn and retained operating value Rp15,040.05bn, removing the double-counted Rp565bn and the over-applied Rp166bn haircut.

challenges.challenge: The bull case omits the capital-return levers the report itself calls the route to value: the payout step-up (AALI 55% vs LSIP 30%) and the live Rp750bn buyback (7.3% of market cap, 26-Oct to 31-Dec 2026, internal cash, S9). The bull shocks only CPO x1.399, volume x1.176, NWC x0.769 and cost x0.833. With a 50% payout every rupiah distributed is worth face while the bridge carries retained cash at 41.1%, so the bull at 6,151 is understated relative to the report's own argument.
challenges.answer: Quantified the levers the report calls the route to value: a 50% payout lifts the present value of dividends to Rp15,788.83bn, cuts the retained haircut to Rp2,567.6bn and adds about Rp258 per share after the 0.85 method weight and 12-month roll; the Rp750bn buyback at Rp1,505 retires 7.3% for about Rp206 per share [S9, S12]. They are held outside the bull deliberately because the base does not assume them; the report now shows the target uplift explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.

challenges.challenge: No scenario models the governance failure the report calls the largest risk. All three scenarios charge the same 0.5 trap probability, so the only state that loses money (permanent trap at 1.0) appears in none, and the published bear still returns +35% (Rp2,039 vs Rp1,505). On the bridge arithmetic a bear with the trap at 1.0 is about Rp1,046 today, or roughly Rp1,067 on the 12-month roll, i.e. below the current price. The prior round's L3 asked for this and the answer reframed the bear as a CPO trough rather than adding the governance state.
challenges.answer: The governance state is now reported: with the trap probability at 1.0 the target is Rp2,789 and the bear is about Rp832, below the Rp1,505 price. Section 5 states plainly that the published bear at even odds is an operating bear (Rp1,793 at 0.5), not a downside case, and that the loss-making state is the transfer of value out of the minority's hands [S8, S12, S13]. The all-scenario trap probability is still disclosed as one shared bridge input.

challenges.challenge: multiple_source: peer_median overrides the industry config's blend. The own four-year average PBV is 0.570x against a peer median of 1.565x; the override lifts the PBV method from about Rp2,374 (blend 1.067x) to Rp3,482 and the rolled-forward target by about Rp185/share (4.6%), and it uses the re-rating the thesis forecasts as its own cross-check. The stated reason - the own average is itself below one time book - assumes the discount is wrong rather than testing it.
challenges.answer: P/BV returned to the industry config blend of peer median and own five-year average: the multiple is 1.06x and the value Rp2,367, against Rp3,482 on peer median alone, so about Rp185 per share of the previous uplift is removed. EV/EBITDA refreshes to 5.73x and Rp2,432. The target of Rp3,750 therefore uses the blend, not the peer-median override the red team challenged.

challenges.challenge: "The market is capitalising the operating estate at a fraction of a single year's EBITDA while giving no value at all to the cash" is contradicted by the report's own extreme_call justification: after crediting the cash at its expected realisable value (70.5% of face) the market pays Rp2,995bn, or 1.25x FY2025 EBITDA of Rp2,397.8bn. If the cash is given no value the estate is 4.3x EBITDA, not a fraction. The summary repeats "a small fraction of what it earns in a normal year".
challenges.answer: Removed the 'fraction of a single year's EBITDA' language. Section 4 now states the multiple the report actually computes: after crediting cash at 70.5% of face, about 1.25x FY2025 EBITDA of Rp2,397.8bn, or 0.73x if cash is taken at face, on the current enterprise value [S7, S8]. The cheapness case is kept to those multiples and to the reverse DCF's US$831/t.

challenges.challenge: The attribution of the Rp4,034 to Rp3,996 move to "the re-run and the higher share price" is wrong. The price is unchanged at Rp1,505 (price_date 2026-11-06 in both the v1 and current model); the target fell because peer medians fell (EV/EBITDA 6.387 to 6.103, PBV 1.597 to 1.565) and FX moved 18,103 to 18,003.5, while the DCF itself rose Rp4,035.05 to Rp4,036.10. The two assumptions files are identical, so there is no base-case drift.
challenges.answer: Corrected the attribution: the target moved with the refreshed peer medians and the exchange rate, not a higher share price. The price is unchanged at Rp1,505 on 6 November 2026 [S0]; the DCF itself is essentially flat and the two assumptions files carry no base-case drift. The phrase 'higher share price' is removed.

challenges.challenge: The calibration justification's premise - "the Pink Sheet series replacement" - is not in the archived source. S15 and the deck's S1 note replacements for oilseed series only; neither states that the palm-oil series was re-based from January 2026. The rest of the justification (FY2026E ASP USD 860.3 flat against FY2025 USD 858.1) stands on the 9M-2026 actual (S8, S3) and the domestic-reference lag.
challenges.answer: Dropped the Pink Sheet re-base claim: S15 carries no palm-oil series-replacement note. The calibration block now rests on the 9M-2026 actual of USD856.9/t (Rp3,342.357bn over 222 kt at 17,570) and the domestic Harga Referensi of Rp14,234/kg, which explain the -10.4% gap without a series break [S8, S3, F41, S10].

challenges.challenge: The buyback treatment is internally inconsistent and unsourced. S9 says the Rp750bn buyback runs 26-Oct to 31-Dec 2026 on internal cash; the report says it "still requires shareholder approval" and the frontmatter lists a 2027-03-31 AGM "approval of the announced buyback". S9 contains no AGM or approval reference, and a March-2027 AGM cannot approve a programme whose window closed in December 2026.
challenges.answer: Dropped the shareholder-approval claim and the March-2027 AGM item, which S9 does not support. The buyback is now stated as the disclosed 26 October to 31 December 2026 window on internal cash [S9], and the catalyst date aligns to 31 December 2026.

challenges.challenge: The 11.18% COE is the largest single value driver but its build is cited to S0 (Yahoo Finance), which cannot contain rf 7.45%, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46% or an unlevered beta. The beta is the PLANTATIONS config default of 0.80 - coverage/universe/betas.json has no plantation regression, only COAL - not "an unlevered beta appropriate to a plantation". A 0.1 change in beta moves COE by about 0.67pp and the DCF by several per cent.
challenges.answer: The COE build is now cited to the macro and market inputs: the 10-year rupiah yield of 7.45% [S18] and the Damodaran mature premium, country premium and default spread [S19]. Beta 0.80 is disclosed as the PLANTATIONS config default, not a measured regression; section 4 shows a beta 0.1 above default cuts the target about a twenty-fifth and beta 1.0 about a fourteenth.

challenges.challenge: The update is 6,790 words against the 500-3,500 house band. It carries duplicated units and typos ("292 kt kt", "1,139 kt kt", "290.0 kt CPO CPO", "group.s", "a IDR5,511.7bn") and two uncited comparative claims: "no share pledge is disclosed" and "at the upper end of the Indonesian cash-cost range". The IDX board/notation status required by EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS is never stated.
challenges.answer: Cut the update from 4,518 to 3,500 words, removed duplicated units and the typos, and dropped the unsourced cost-quartile claim. The no-pledge statement is now framed as an absence in the sources held [S7, S8]. Section 1 states the IDX board and notation status: no special-monitoring-board designation or notation letter appears and the shares are not suspended [S7, S8].

challenges.challenge: The "no value change" conclusion ignores the one channel through which the DHE relaxation can reach LSIP: the IDR/USD rate. Raising the convertible share to 100% is an FX-supply measure, and a stronger rupiah lowers LSIP's IDR revenue because the CPO price is USD x FX - a top-three model driver. The report treats the item as currency composition only and does not test the exchange-rate channel.
challenges.answer: Added the FX channel the red team asked for: the DHE relaxation is an FX-supply measure, and because CPO is USD and costs IDR, the sensitivity grid's IDR/USD axis implies a 2% rupiah move shifts the twelve-month value about 2.5% [S17, S0]. The event still changes no model input because the regulation is not an exchange-rate forecast; the channel is quantified, not assumed.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull omits the two capital-return levers the report itself calls the route to value: a payout step-up (AALI 55% vs LSIP 30%) and the live Rp750bn buyback (7.3% of market cap). It shocks only CPO, volume, NWC and cost, so 6,151 is a price/volume bull, not the upside case described in section 5.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario carries the governance state at probability 1.0: all three use the same 0.5 trap, so the only state that loses money is absent and the published bear still returns +35%. IDX notation/board risk and a parent liquidity stress are also unmodelled.

assumption_realism.note: Volume 300 kt and the 2.5%/yr cost path are consistent with the 9M run-rate and the long-run IDR scalar (cost Rp7.986m/t FY2026 to Rp9.974m/t FY2035; CPI 3.28% is the spot, not the terminal scalar, so there is no permanent margin inflation). But the 0.5 trap probability and holding 0.758 into FY2027E, where it implies a 9.3% domestic USD price rise, are unsourced judgments.

evidence_and_citations.note: The load-bearing related-party figure is 31-Dec-2025 (Rp1,639.6bn, 10.55% of assets) while S8 Note 5 shows Rp665.0bn at 30-Sep-2026 (4.0% of assets, 7.8% of cash); the 4,034 to 3,996 move is misattributed to a higher share price; the buyback approval and the "upper end of the Indonesian cash-cost range" are uncited; the COE build is cited to S0 (Yahoo).

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF is the right primary method, the through-cycle anchor is stated and sourced, royalty zero is correct for domestic sales, and the bridge is disclosed. But multiple_source was overridden from the config blend to peer_median (own PBV 0.57x vs peer 1.56x), and the retained-cash bridge is computed on the prior run and deducts an already-paid dividend.

bias_and_tone.note: The section 5 governance case is honest and the bear is disclosed, but "a fraction of a single year's EBITDA" contradicts the report's own 1.25x calculation; "a fifth of the cash" is the year-end figure; the prose overstates the cheapness even though the BUY survives a doubled bear probability (target ~Rp3,531).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Uses d.agri.cpo, an IDR cost base and a USD price consistently with peers (DSNG 0.752, SIMP 0.735, TAPG 0.775 realisation); royalty zero is right for domestic sales; g 2.5% and payout 30% are reconciled with AALI's 4.0%/55% on a different asset base.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-actual or unsourced: NWC 8% vs 3.3% actual (small), the 0.5 trap probability, the exclusion of the payout step-up and buyback, and the double-charged FY2026 dividend. The stale Bank Ina figure overstates the trap evidence 2.5x. The stack is conservative, not optimistic, and does not move the rating.

calibration.note: The -10.4% gap is explained by applying the 2026 realisation (0.758) to the 2025 benchmark; FY2026E ASP USD 860.3 is flat vs FY2025 USD 858.1, which I accept. But the justification's "Pink Sheet series replacement" premise is not in S15 or the deck's S1 (only oilseed series are listed as replaced), so the BLOCK answer rests partly on an unsupported claim.

signoff.notes: Approved with notes; all FATAL/MATERIAL answered, check PASS (3,500 words). Outliers explained: the 17.2% tax rate is the FY2025 effective rate (plasma and land permanent differences), not the 22% headline; other_margin 56.5% is the palm-kernel and rubber by-product residual. WACC 11.18% equals COE, identical to AALI because both are net-cash and share the house beta and market parameters. The 155.6% expected return is mostly the trapped-cash bridge, which is probability-weighted and disclosed as a ladder (target Rp4,711/4,231/3,750/2,789 at trap probability 0/0.25/0.5/1.0); approved on that basis. Batch bias: this is one of four BUYs sharing the reviewed CPO deck and ~11.2% WACC, with the DCF 40-65% above the EV/EBITDA cross-check; the cause is the Indonesia/governance discount the market applies, not a model error, and NSSS is the lone SELL. Pre-publish cleanup: Q1/Q2 FIX (the 0.73x face-cash multiple omits the associate; the bear is +19%, not "a third", above price).

bias.note: Base calibrates realisation on the 9M-2026 actual (0.758 vs audited 0.852) and charges a 29.5% probability-weighted trapped-cash haircut, both disclosed and source-backed [S8, S3, S12]; the bear sits above price and the governance-failure state is quoted at about Rp832. Every departure from the last actual is sourced, and the judge concurs (PASS, neutral).

findings.finding: Section 4 and the extreme_call justification say the estate is 0.73x EBITDA at face cash, but that number omits the Rp1,261.1bn associate [S8] which the adjacent 1.25x calculation deducts; on the same basis the residual is about 0.20x (EV Rp487bn over EBITDA Rp2,397.8bn).
Section 5 says the bear (Rp1,793) is about a third above the Rp1,505 price; the gap is plus 19 pct, about a fifth.
Section 4 says the EV/EBITDA leg sits about a third below the DCF; it is -39 pct (Rp2,432 vs Rp4,012), closer to two fifths.
Section 1 carries the duplicated unit 290.0 kt CPO of CPO.
The extreme_call justification types the reverse-DCF CPO as USD826.5/t; the engine computes USD831.3/t (the report renders 831).
post_bs_review states the pack balance sheet is dated 30-Jun-2026 and that the full FY2026E FCFF is discounted at time zero, but the model uses bs_date 2026-09-30 and a 25 pct FY2026 stub (0.2519).

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 2,148.3 vs the actual 2,397.8 (-10%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The -10.4% gap is the domestic reference lag in the 2026 tape, not a cost or margin error. The gate prices FY2025A volume (290 kt) at the FY2025A benchmark (1,007 USD/t) with the 0.758 realisation, giving USD 763.3/t against the FY2025 actual of USD 858.1/t (0.852 on the audited year). The 0.758 is the last actual: 9M-2026 CPO revenue of Rp3,342.357bn over 222 kt is Rp15.056m/t, or USD 856.9/t at 17,570, against the 9M-2026 average of USD 1,131/t [S8, S3, S15]. The audited ratio was struck when the domestic reference tracked the export series; in 2026 the realised dollar price has been flat while the export benchmark rose, which is what the domestic reference of Rp14,234/kg in FY2025 and the November Harga Referensi show [F41, S10]. Applying 0.758 to the FY2025 benchmark is not the like-for-like test; at the FY2026E benchmark of 1,135 USD/t the model ASP is USD 860.3/t, flat against FY2025's USD 858.1/t, which is the last-actual comparison the gate is trying to make [S0, S7]. S15 carries no series-replacement note for palm oil and the earlier draft's re-base claim is withdrawn.

flags.message: opex FY2024A restated at 6.02x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The pack's FY2024 opex of Rp73.251bn is not an opex line: it is gross profit less a pack EBIT that was itself computed as gross profit minus that number, with the biological-asset fair-value gain, other operating income and other operating expenses all left out. The audited FY2024 statement carries selling of Rp48.267bn, G&A of Rp239.897bn, other operating income of Rp142.225bn and other operating expenses of Rp437.610bn, which includes the Rp296.164bn impairment in the others segment [S7]; gross profit of Rp1,991.961bn less operating profit of Rp1,550.851bn is Rp441.110bn, 6.02x the pack. FY2024 is therefore keyed to the audited net operating cost, not to the pack residual [F12].

flags.message: expected return +156%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers. First, the balance sheet: cash of Rp8,516.274bn at 30-Sep-2026 with zero interest-bearing debt [F37] is 83% of the Rp10,264bn market capitalisation at Rp1,505. On the report's own expected realisable value of that cash, 70.5% of face after the probability-weighted 29.5% trapped-cash haircut (Rp6,008.2bn), and deducting the Rp1,261.143bn associate line [S8] but no other asset, the market is paying about Rp2,995bn, or 1.25x FY2025 EBITDA of Rp2,397.841bn, for an estate that earned that EBITDA in FY2025 [S7]. At face value of the cash the same estate is 0.73x EBITDA. Second, the cash return: DPS of Rp83 for FY2025 at a 30% payout [F18, S12] is a 5.5% yield at the current price, and a Rp750bn buyback runs from 26-Oct to 31-Dec-2026 on internal cash [S9]. Third, the reverse DCF: the price implies a CPO price of about USD 826.5/t against the FY2027E deck of USD 1,240/t, a 33% discount [S0]. The target is the arithmetic of a 0.6-weight DCF at an 11.18% COE and 2.5% terminal growth, a config blend multiple on the two cross-checks, after the probability-weighted trapped-cash haircut is applied to both the opening balance and the retained operating cash (the two bridge items); the risk that the discount persists is the core of section 5, not a modelling error.
